Run **korejan's build** — it bakes in the engine-level optimizations automatically (NVENC + networking + shaders), then apply a settings profile tuned for a 4080S on a wired Quest 3. The optimizations split into two buckets: *automatic* (you get them just by running the build) and *settings you set*.

## 1. Automatic — just by running korejan (NVIDIA/Windows/wired-relevant)
These are baked into the build, no config needed:
- **NVENC path**: reuses frame-buffer allocations, removes redundant frame-packet copies/allocs, latest NVENC SDK 13, 1.1-frame VBV buffer (lower latency), configurable reframes
- **Networking** (matters even on wired for CPU/latency): "remove network temp allocations and extra copies", stream-socket packet-size opts, `nanors` Reed-Solomon (faster FEC), bincode v2
- **Client/Quest 3**: sRGB linearization shader opt, Vulkan shader opts, Mediacodec low-latency decoder flags enabled by default, input-update opt

## 2. Encoder settings to set (4080 Super has huge headroom — spend it on quality)
| Setting | Set to | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Codec | **HEVC** | AV1 not in korejan/buggy on Quest 3; wired bitrate makes AV1's efficiency edge moot |
| 10-bit encoding | **ON** | HEVC Main10; Ada encodes + Quest 3 decodes it; kills color banding |
| Encoder quality preset | **Quality** (default is Speed) | 4080S encodes a frame far under budget |
| NVENC tuning | **UltraLowLatency** (default LowLatency) | lowest encode latency |
| Multi-pass | QuarterResolution (keep) | Full only if chasing max quality and OK eating latency |
| Rate control | **CBR** (keep) | correct for streaming |
| Adaptive quant | Spatial (keep) | good default |
| VBAQ / CABAC entropy | **ignore** | VBAQ is AMD-only; CABAC is H264-only — N/A for NVIDIA+HEVC |
| Bitrate | **150–200 Mbps fixed** | wired headroom; don't exceed ~200 — Quest 3's HEVC decoder has a ceiling |

## 3. Latency / network — wired-specific
- **Adaptive bitrate: OFF** — stable wired link doesn't need it; use the fixed high bitrate above
- **FEC: OFF** *if true USB tether* (no packet loss → FEC is pure wasted latency). **Keep ON if your Quest is actually on Wi-Fi** with only the PC wired — see caveat below
- **Extra latency mode: OFF**
- **Latency target**: korejan defaults 12 ms; you can lower it on a clean wired link

## 4. Quest 3 / display
- **Refresh**: 90 Hz (quality headroom) or 120 Hz (smoothness) — 4080S handles either
- **Render resolution**: bump to ~1.0–1.2× — you have the GPU + bandwidth budget
- **Foveated rendering**: keep ON but lower strength (bandwidth to spare); turn off only if you want max peripheral clarity
- **Realtime decoder request**: ON

## ⚠️ One thing that flips the advice — what "wired" means
- **USB-C cable tether** (Quest plugged into PC, ALVR over USB) → FEC off, push bitrate, lowest latency. ✅ all above applies.
- **PC on Ethernet but Quest on Wi-Fi** → keep **FEC ON** and **adaptive bitrate ON**; the wireless hop still drops packets.

## A) Encode-side — NVIDIA Split Frame Encoding (the one for your 4080S)
This is the relevant one for you: the AD103 die in the 4080 Super has **2 NVENC engines**, and SFE splits each frame into horizontal strips encoded in parallel across them — roughly halving the *encode* stage of the latency pipeline.

**Status: requested, never implemented as a feature.** Issue **#2444** asks for it — and it has **0 comments, no PR, no fork wired it up** (code search across the fork network is empty for `NV_ENC_SPLIT_ENCODE_MODE`).

**But** — korejan already passes the field on AUTO:
```cpp
// korejan: VideoEncoderNVENC.cpp:160
initializeParams.splitEncodeMode = NV_ENC_SPLIT_AUTO_MODE;
```
`AUTO` means the *driver* enables split-frame only when its conditions are met: HEVC (not H264), 2+ NVENC engines, and **vertical resolution > 2112px**. So on korejan, at high render resolution, split-frame already engages automatically on your card. What nobody has done is expose the **forced** modes from #2444 — `NV_ENC_SPLIT_AUTO_FORCED_MODE` / `NV_ENC_SPLIT_TWO_FORCED_MODE` — which force it on *below* 2112px, where most VR resolutions actually sit and where it'd help latency most.

That's a genuinely promising, ~10-line win for your exact hardware: add a settings toggle + set the mode in `VideoEncoderNVENC.cpp`. The API enum is already in korejan's SDK 13 header (`nvEncodeAPI.h:2215`).

## B) Decode/network-side — intra-frame pipelining / partial-frame decode
**Status: tried experimentally (#2436), didn't pan out.** `@vosk` actually prototyped `BUFFER_FLAG_PARTIAL_FRAME` to pipeline receive→copy→decode per-shard:
- Reduced socket jitter, but **time-to-photon measured *worse***
- MediaCodec ran out of input buffers → forced re-merging shards into a contiguous buffer anyway
- Vendor MediaCodec didn't reliably honor the partial-frame flag (a Xiaomi test device rendered only the top strip)
- Maintainer (zmerp) verdict: micro-optimization worth **~1–2ms at most** (one frame copy); *"best option is not to mess with mediacodec."* Suggested compromise: split into a fixed packet count ≤ max MediaCodec input buffers — never finished.

This one matters less for you anyway: on a wired link you're not jitter-bound, so the upside is tiny.

## Takeaway for your setup
- **Worth doing:** the **encode-side forced split toggle** (#2444). Nobody's built it, it's small, and it targets your dual-NVENC 4080S directly. Biggest latency lever of the two.
- **Skip:** decode-side partial-frame pipelining — already explored, net-negative, vendor-fragile.
